examples.knowledge_point: Integrating Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions With Linear Arguments
examples.worked_solution:
If we let $u=6x+\dfrac \pi 3,$ then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 6\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x =\dfrac 1 6\, \textrm d u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 5\operatorname{csc}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{cot}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}x & =5\int \operatorname{csc}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{cot}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\int \operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{6}\int \operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{5}{6}\operatorname{csc}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{5}{6}\operatorname{csc}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})+C\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
If we let $u=\frac{\pi x}{4},$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\pi }{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{4}{\pi }\,\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\pi /2$ |

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{4})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot \frac{4}{\pi }\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{4}{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{4}{\pi }(1-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{\pi }\end{aligned}
$$
